clue.text: Food costing a lot, though not a soup

parts.note: chow is slang for food

indicators.note: not tells us to leave out the letter a from the word before it

parts.note: dear means expensive

explanation.surface: A diner remarks that a dish is pricey, though at least it isn't soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food' wants to be the definition, but the answer is the soup. 'not' removes A from DEAR, leaving DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Chowder is a thick, chunky North American soup, often made with clams or fish.

clue.text: Quiet person, brought up to repress merest hint of enthusiasm, rose with difficulty

parts.note: a clam is someone who keeps quiet, clams up

indicators.note: to repress means to hold something in, so the hint goes inside

parts.note: bred means raised or brought up

indicators.note: merest hint of picks only the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A shy person, raised to suppress any enthusiasm, struggles to get up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet person' as CLAM comes from clamming up; 'to repress' tucks the E inside, giving BERED.
explanation.definitionFit: To clamber is to climb awkwardly using hands and feet, rising with effort.

clue.text: Vessel offloading second-rate grain

indicators.note: offloading means the letter for second-rate is unloaded from the vessel word

parts.note: a boat is a vessel
B, as in B-grade or B-movie, means second-rate

explanation.surface: A ship unloads a cargo of poor-quality grain.
explanation.definitionFit: Oats are a cereal crop, a kind of grain.

clue.text: Rodents, millions, coming in to attack grain

parts.note: to do someone is slang for attacking them

indicators.note: coming in to means the millions letter enters the other words

parts.note: rice is a cereal grain
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: Rodents in their millions descend to attack a grain store.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'do' someone is slang for beating them up; 'coming in to' places the M within the grain.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormice are small rodents known for hibernating for long periods.

clue.text: Some illumination around endless religious service? It's not often seen

indicators.note: around means the light word wraps the shortened service word

parts.note: a ray is a beam, a bit of light

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the service word is cut

parts.note: a rite is a religious ceremony

explanation.surface: Light streams round a rare religious service, something seldom seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' leaves RIT; 'around' puts the light around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rarity is something uncommon, encountered only seldom.

clue.text: Have another try, but after rebuilding fortress

indicators.note: after places the rebuilt letters behind the first piece

parts.note: to redo something is to have another go at it

indicators.note: rebuilding tells us the letters of but are rearranged

explanation.surface: An attacker resolves to try again, but only after the siege works are rebuilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' looks like a link word but is the anagram fodder; 'rebuilding' gives UBT and 'after' sets it last.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small outlying fort or defensive stronghold, a kind of fortress.

clue.text: Armed force keeps on ignoring hoax trains

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

indicators.note: ignoring means the hoax word is left out

parts.note: continues means keeps on
a con is a trick or hoax

explanation.surface: An army unit persists with its work, ignoring a hoax about the trains.
explanation.walkthrough: RE (Royal Engineers) is a British Army corps; 'ignoring' drops CON from CONTINUES, leaving TINUES.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the train of attendants following an important person, so trains in that sense.

clue.text: "Suffocated, in a way" medic admitted

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
owned, as in owned up to, means admitted

explanation.surface: A doctor confesses that someone was suffocated in some manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Drowning is death by being unable to breathe under water, one particular way to suffocate.

clue.text: Swirling nebula later having fixed form

indicators.note: swirling suggests the letters are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A swirling nebula later settles into a fixed shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unalterable cannot be changed, so its form stays fixed.

clue.text: Affected depth in river

parts.note: twee means affectedly quaint

explanation.surface: Someone gets precious about how deep a river is.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tweed is a river forming part of the border between England and Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tweed is a river in the Scottish Borders, flowing into the North Sea at Berwick.

clue.text: A lot of concern about temperature in part of church

indicators.note: about means the shortened word goes around the letter for temperature
a lot of, not all, so the last letter of the word for concern is dropped

parts.note: alarm is a feeling of worried concern

explanation.surface: Someone frets about temperature in a chilly part of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' trims ALARM to ALAR, which goes 'about' T.
explanation.definitionFit: The altar is the table at the east end of a church where communion is celebrated.

clue.text: A lot of tax one applied to beer has some justification

indicators.note: a lot of, not all, so the final letter of the word for tax is cut

parts.note: a rate is a local tax
I is the Roman numeral for one
on, as in a coat of paint put on a wall
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A heavy duty on beer is said to have some justification behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' cuts RATE to RAT; then come I, ON and ALE in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A rationale is the reasoning or set of reasons offered to justify a decision.

clue.text: Producer of counterfeit cash, say, ready to go in Gloucestershire village

parts.note: a bad mint would be one turning out fake money
on, as in a show that is on and ready to start

explanation.surface: A forger, ready for action, is hiding out in a country village.
explanation.walkthrough: BADMINTON is an English village in Gloucestershire, famous for its horse trials and as the namesake of the racket sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is a real village in the county of Gloucestershire, home of Badminton House.

clue.text: Board, diligent, working with an opening for business

indicators.note: working implies the letters are worked into a new arrangement
opening for picks the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A diligent company board works on an opening for new business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' looks like directors, but it is the table. 'working' rearranges DILIGENT, AN and B.
explanation.definitionFit: Board is an old word for a table, especially one where meals are served, as in bed and board.

clue.text: Rejected working with hooligan of repute

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word for working is read backwards

parts.note: on, as in a machine that is on and running
a Ted, short for Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth often seen as a hooligan

explanation.surface: A troublemaker is turned away after working with a hooligan of some repute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' turns ON into NO. A Teddy boy (TED) was a 1950s British youth-culture figure in Edwardian-style dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone noted is well known or celebrated, which is to be of repute.

clue.text: Errand-boy who's done with escaping?

definitions.meaning: a lad sent to carry messages and run errands
British slang for fleeing, so one who has done that is described here

explanation.surface: An errand-boy is suspected of having run off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do a runner' is British slang for leaving in a hurry, often without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: A messenger who carries errands is a classic sense, and the slang phrase gives the second reading.

clue.text: Brought about stop before entering road

indicators.note: entering means the words for stop and before go inside the road abbreviation

parts.note: an end is a stop or finish
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A driver comes to a stop before pulling onto the road.
explanation.walkthrough: ERE is an archaic word for before; 'entering' places it and the stop word between the R and D.
explanation.definitionFit: To render something is to cause it to become so, as in rendered helpless; brought about is a synonym.

clue.text: What determines whether a habit is good or bad?

definitions.text: What determines whether a habit is good or bad?

parts.words: What determines whether a habit is good or bad?
parts.note: a habit is a garment as well as a custom, so the rules on acceptable clothing decide what is fit to wear

explanation.surface: A moralist asks what decides whether a habit is a good one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' reads as a routine, but it is clothing, as in a nun's or riding habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress code is a set of rules on what clothing is acceptable in a place.

clue.text: Locums: doctors, including one chasing rising amounts of money

indicators.note: chasing means the doctors piece comes after the money piece
rising, in a down clue, means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: pots are large sums of money, as in pots of cash

indicators.note: including means the doctors' letters hold the letter for one

parts.note: GPs are general practitioners, family doctors
A, as in a single one

explanation.surface: Locum doctors are seen chasing ever-increasing fees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns POTS into STOP; GPS 'including' A gives GAPS, 'chasing' STOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Locums are temporary stand-ins covering for absent doctors, which is what stopgaps are.

clue.text: Row with Government is followed by crazy characters

indicators.note: is followed by places the next word after what comes before it

parts.note: a din is a noisy row
bats is slang for mad

explanation.surface: A noisy row with the Government is followed by some crazy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' looks like it describes the characters, but it gives BATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingbats are decorative typographic symbols, and also an informal term for silly people, so characters fits both.

clue.text: Name hellish pit reprobate's seen around

indicators.note: seen around means the base word encloses the others

parts.note: a reprobate is base, morally low, with the 's standing for is

indicators.note: hellish suggests the letters of pit are thrown into chaos

explanation.surface: A wicked person is seen around a pit of hell, as if naming it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hellish' gives PTI; 'reprobate's' is read as 'reprobate is', an adjective; 'seen around' wraps it.
explanation.definitionFit: To baptise someone is to give them a name at a christening.

clue.text: Out of practice, having to carry book to be sure

indicators.note: having to carry means the word for out of practice holds the book letter

parts.note: stale describes someone who has lost freshness through lack of practice

explanation.surface: A rusty performer has to carry the script to be sure of the lines.
explanation.walkthrough: STALE is 'having to carry' B, giving STA-B-LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stable means steady and secure, as sure footing is firm and dependable.

clue.text: Couple taking up work on farm, appearing in book

indicators.note: appearing in means the reversed farm word goes inside the book word

parts.note: a tome is a large book

indicators.note: taking up, in a down clue, means the word is read upwards

parts.note: to sow seed is farm work

explanation.surface: A pair take up farm work, and appear in a book about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking up' turns SOW into WOS, 'appearing in' TOME.
explanation.definitionFit: A twosome is a pair of people, a couple.

clue.text: Special equipment to make furniture

parts.note: tools are equipment

explanation.surface: Special equipment is needed to make a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Stools are simple seats without backs, items of furniture.

clue.text: Work to keep new reservists ready for deployment

indicators.note: to keep means the work letters hold the others inside

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work
the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A job is set up to keep new reserve soldiers ready to be sent out.
explanation.walkthrough: OP is 'to keep' N and TA. The TA (Territorial Army) was Britain's army reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: On tap means available whenever needed, like beer drawn from a cask.

clue.text: Australia has a specific beach attraction (supposedly)

parts.note: Oz is a nickname for Australia
one, as in one particular person or thing

explanation.surface: Australia has a particular beach attraction, or so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Sea air was popularly believed to be rich in this gas and good for health, hence 'supposedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaside air was traditionally thought to be full of a bracing gas, a supposed draw of the beach.

clue.text: Way information is suppressed by large-scale promoters of disease

parts.note: a path is a way

indicators.note: is suppressed by means the information is held down within the letters for large-scale

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, very large
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Information on a way of spreading illness is suppressed by large-scale disease promoters.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a clothing-size label; 'is suppressed by' holds the information word inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathogens are bacteria, viruses and other agents that cause illness, so they promote it.

clue.text: Lab too big for change? It has to come through

indicators.note: for change says these letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A laboratory is too large and needs changing, says someone pushing it through.
explanation.definitionFit: An obbligato is an instrumental part that must not be omitted, so it has to be heard in performance.

clue.text: Name encountered in circles in part of New Zealand

indicators.note: in tells us the name word sits inside the pair of rings

parts.note: each O is the shape of a circle
a tag is a name or label

explanation.surface: A name is met in some circles somewhere in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: TAG sits 'in' two Os, the 'circles'.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago is a region in the south of New Zealand's South Island, centred on Dunedin.

clue.text: A description of fairly quiet music — not what you'd get from this!

definitions.text: not what you'd get from this!

parts.note: mp, mezzo piano, is the musical marking for moderately soft

explanation.surface: A musical marking for fairly soft playing is the opposite of what this gadget gives.
explanation.walkthrough: The device in question makes music loud, so quiet music is the last thing it delivers.
explanation.definitionFit: An amplifier boosts volume, so a quiet sound is exactly what it does not produce.

clue.text: Players avoiding weather around the old holes

indicators.note: around means the shortened weather word is placed around the old article
avoiding means the word for players is left out of the weather word

parts.note: the elements are the weather, wind and rain
men are the players in a team
ye is an old form of the

explanation.surface: Players skip bad weather and head for the old holes, as at a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weather' is 'the elements'; 'avoiding' leaves ELETS, and 'around' wraps it round the archaic YE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyelets are small reinforced holes for laces or cords to pass through.

clue.text: Expensive romance, though without one church feature

parts.note: steep prices are high

indicators.note: without means the letter for one is dropped from the word for romance

parts.note: to romance is to tell fanciful untruths, to lie
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An expensive love affair, though without a single church feature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'romance' as a verb means to embellish or fib, giving LIE; 'without' removes I, leaving LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall tower and spire of a church.
